title: India's Weakest Monsoon in 11 Years Is Threatening to Derail the Post-Oil Rally — and a Super El Niño Could Make It Worse
excerpt: Rainfall is running 43% below average, sugar prices are surging, and Citigroup warns El Niño could cost the global economy up to $7 trillion. India has drawn up contingency plans for over 300 districts — but investors are asking whether the damage is already priced in.
body:
Just as Indian markets were breathing easy after crude oil prices tumbled back to pre-war levels, a new threat has emerged from the sky — or rather, from the conspicuous absence of rain.

India's cumulative monsoon rainfall is running approximately 43 percent below the long-term average as of late June, putting the country on track for what the India Meteorological Department warns could be the weakest monsoon in 11 years. The agency has lowered its seasonal forecast to just 90 percent of the long-term average, down from an earlier projection of 92 percent — and the week ending July 2 is expected to bring continued below-normal rainfall.

For an economy where nearly half of farmland lacks irrigation and roughly half the population depends on agriculture for its livelihood, the monsoon isn't just a weather event. It is a macroeconomic variable with the power to move inflation, rural consumption, GDP growth, and — inevitably — equity markets.

## The El Niño Wildcard

The monsoon deficit alone would be concerning. But layered on top is the confirmed emergence of an El Niño weather pattern — a warming of sea surface temperatures across the equatorial Pacific that historically disrupts monsoon patterns across South and Southeast Asia.

The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) is now predicting a more than 95 percent chance that El Niño has started and will continue through at least March 2027. More alarmingly, there is a 67 percent probability of a "very strong" or super El Niño forming by the end of 2026.

Citigroup economists, led by Nathan Sheets, warned in a recent research note that a strong El Niño could inflict between $3 trillion and $5 trillion in global economic losses over five years — roughly 2.7 to 3.2 percent of global GDP. In a super El Niño scenario, losses could reach $7 trillion, or 6.4 percent of GDP. The 1997–98 El Niño, the most economically destructive on record, cost approximately $5.7 trillion.

"While one supply shock is abating, another one may be around the corner," the Citigroup note said, referring to the easing of the Iran-related oil price spike.

Japan's Meteorological Agency has already confirmed that an El Niño pattern has formed. The downstream effects are expected to curb rainfall in Brazil, India, and Thailand — the world's three largest sugar-producing regions — simultaneously.

## Sugar Prices Are Already Surging



> **"The 1997–98 El Niño, the most economically destructive on record, cost approximately $5.7 trillion."**


The commodity markets are not waiting for confirmation. NY world sugar futures climbed more than 3.3 percent in a single session last week, hitting a two-week high, while London white sugar jumped 4.4 percent to a 2.75-month high. The driver: fears that weak monsoon rains in India, the world's second-largest sugar producer, will lower sugarcane yields and reduce the harvest.

Sugar trader Czarnikow has already cut its global 2026/27 sugar balance estimate from a surplus of 1.4 million metric tonnes to a deficit of 100,000 MT. The Indian Sugar and Bio-energy Manufacturers Association (ISMA) has revised India's 2025/26 production forecast downward to 32 million metric tonnes, from an earlier estimate of 32.4 MMT.

For India's economy, the implications extend well beyond sugar. A weak monsoon typically drives up prices of vegetables, pulses, and other food staples, stoking the food inflation that the Reserve Bank of India has spent years trying to tame. Nuvama, a domestic brokerage, warned in a note that the combination of residual oil price effects and a deficit monsoon raises the spectre of stagflation — sluggish growth with rising prices.

## The Government's Contingency Playbook


![India Meteorological Department — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f2/IMD_Mausam_Bhavan_Headquarters_New_Delhi_2017.jpg)


India's farm minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan has chaired an emergency meeting with state farm ministers and scientists, announcing contingency plans for more than 300 districts deemed vulnerable to monsoon shortfall. Of these, 111 have been classified as high priority, with less than a quarter of their farmland irrigated.

States have been advised to encourage farmers in rain-fed areas to shift to short-duration, less water-intensive crops — pulses, millets, and oilseeds rather than rice and sugarcane. The government has also directed states to repair water-harvesting infrastructure, including ponds, check dams, and reservoirs.

The good news: India has ample stocks of rice and wheat from two consecutive years of above-normal rainfall, providing a buffer against any immediate food security crisis. India's irrigated farmland has also been rising steadily, with 55 percent of cultivated land now having assured water supply — a significant improvement from a decade ago.

## Goldman Sachs Still Likes the Story

In a contrarian move, Goldman Sachs actually *upgraded* its India growth outlook last week, raising its GDP forecast on the back of easing Gulf tensions and lower oil prices. The investment bank noted that India's real GDP grew 7.8 percent year-on-year in Q1 CY2026 — about 50 basis points above its earlier forecast — led by resilient investment activity and robust services sector performance.

Gross fixed capital formation rose to a six-quarter high, and port cargo traffic growth touched a four-month high in May. Goldman Sachs said the US-Iran agreement has "significantly reduced downside risks" by lowering crude prices and easing supply constraints.

But even Goldman flagged the monsoon as the key near-term uncertainty, particularly its implications for rural consumption growth. Weather-related headwinds, including IMD forecasts of heatwaves, remain a concern.

## How to Monsoon-Proof Your Portfolio

VK Vijayakumar of Geojit Investments argues that if the monsoon falls below 90 percent and creates drought-like conditions, both the economy and the stock market will be affected — but a 10 percent deficiency alone, while not ideal, is manageable given ample grain reserves and improving irrigation.

The sectors most exposed to monsoon risk are predictable: FMCG companies with heavy rural revenue exposure, tractor and two-wheeler manufacturers, fertiliser companies, and agri-linked NBFCs. Banks with large rural loan books may also face rising NPAs if farm incomes decline.

On the other side of the trade, sectors that benefit from lower oil prices and are insulated from monsoon effects — pharma, IT services (despite near-term Accenture-driven softness), and select financials — may outperform in a deficit monsoon scenario.

For NRI investors, the actionable framework is relatively clear: maintain equity exposure to India's structural growth story, but tilt sector allocation away from rural-consumption plays and toward export-oriented or urban-demand sectors until the monsoon trajectory becomes clearer by mid-July. Keep an eye on the weekly IMD rainfall data, sugar and vegetable prices, and any RBI commentary on inflation expectations.

The crude oil crisis was a sprint. The monsoon is a marathon. And El Niño just extended the course.

*Sources: Reuters; India Meteorological Department; Citigroup Research (via MarketWatch); Goldman Sachs India Economic Research; Barchart; Livemint / Geojit Investments; ISMA; Czarnikow; NOAA.*
